name: Ethical Egoism
statement: One morally ought always to act in one's own self-interest; the right act maximizes one's own good.
statementAccent: the right act maximizes one's own good
meaning: Ethical egoism is the normative ethical theory that moral agents ought to act in their own self-interest, so that the right action is always the one that maximizes one's own good. It is a prescriptive claim about what one should do, holding that promoting one's own welfare is what morality requires. Ethical egoism must be carefully distinguished from psychological egoism, which is a descriptive claim about human nature, namely that people always do in fact act out of self-interest, that all motivation is ultimately self-interested. Psychological egoism describes how people are motivated; ethical egoism prescribes how they ought to act, and the two are logically independent, though ethical egoism is sometimes, invalidly, argued from psychological egoism. Ethical egoism should also be distinguished from rational egoism, the view that acting in one's self-interest is what is rational, which uses a non-moral sense of ought. In modern times ethical egoism is most associated with Ayn Rand and her philosophy of Objectivism, which defends rational self-interest and treats altruism as destructive, arguing that each person's life is their own end. Ethical egoism has some intuitive appeal but faces serious objections, and it is widely regarded as difficult to defend as a coherent, universal morality.
mechanism: Ethical egoism holds that each person morally ought to do whatever best serves their own interests, so the standard of right action is the agent's own good. To apply it, one asks, of the available actions, which would maximize one's own long-term welfare, and that action is the one morality requires; helping others is right only insofar as it serves one's own interest. Defenders offer several supporting arguments. One route runs from psychological egoism: if people can only act from self-interest, then, on the principle that ought implies can, morality can only require self-interested action; but this inference is invalid, since even if people always do act selfishly it does not follow that they ought to. Other arguments hold that each person is best placed to know and pursue their own interests, that a society of self-interested agents can produce mutual benefit, and that egoism respects individual autonomy. Ayn Rand's version argues that a person's own life is the ultimate value and end, that rational self-interest is virtuous, and that the ethic of altruism and self-sacrifice is destructive. Ethical egoism is distinguished sharply from psychological egoism, which describes motivation, and from rational egoism, which concerns rationality rather than morality. Its central difficulty is whether a doctrine telling each person to pursue their own interest above all can function as a consistent, public morality.

examples.text: Ethical egoism prescribes that one ought to act in one's own self-interest, unlike psychological egoism, which describes that one does.
Ayn Rand defended rational self-interest as virtuous and treated altruism as destructive, the best-known modern ethical egoism.
Ethical egoism concerns what one morally ought to do, while rational egoism concerns what it is rational to do.

whyItMatters: Ethical egoism is an important position in moral philosophy, less because it is widely accepted than because engaging with it clarifies the foundations of ethics. As the theory that one ought always to act in one's own self-interest, it stands as a stark challenge to the common assumption that morality requires concern for others, and confronting it forces careful thought about why, and whether, we have genuine duties to other people. The theory also sharpens crucial distinctions in ethics: between the normative claim of ethical egoism and the descriptive claim of psychological egoism about human motivation, and between moral and merely rational senses of what one ought to do. Its most influential modern form, Ayn Rand's Objectivism, has had significant cultural and political influence, particularly in defending self-interest and criticizing altruism and collectivism. The objections to ethical egoism, including the fallacy of inferring it from psychological egoism, its apparent inconsistency, its inability to serve as a public morality, and James Rachels's charge that favoring one's own interests is arbitrary, are themselves instructive about what a defensible ethics requires. As the challenging view that morality is the pursuit of self-interest, ethical egoism is a valuable foil in moral philosophy.

limits: Ethical egoism faces a battery of serious objections and is widely regarded as difficult to defend. A basic error is inferring ethical egoism from psychological egoism, which commits the is-ought fallacy, since even if people always act selfishly it does not follow that they ought to; moreover, psychological egoism is itself dubious, as people do sometimes act altruistically. Ethical egoism also appears to give inconsistent or contradictory guidance, since it can direct different agents to pursue conflicting interests without any way to resolve the conflict, tending toward a might-makes-right stance. It seems impossible to universalize coherently and cannot readily serve as a public morality, since an egoist cannot consistently advocate that everyone pursue self-interest, including at the egoist's own expense. James Rachels pressed the arbitrariness objection, that singling out one's own interests as specially important is as arbitrary as favoring people with a particular eye color, with no morally relevant difference to justify it. And it conflicts with basic moral intuitions, apparently permitting gross harms to others when self-interested. So ethical egoism robustly asserts that one ought to serve one's own interest, understood as a challenging but widely rejected theory beset by the is-ought fallacy, inconsistency, and the arbitrariness objection.
misreadings: Ethical egoism is not the same as psychological egoism; one is a normative claim that people ought to act selfishly, the other a descriptive claim that they always do, and the former cannot be validly inferred from the latter. It is not merely the sensible advice to look after oneself, but the strong claim that self-interest is the whole of morality. And it is not a well-established theory, since objections about inconsistency, universalizability, and arbitrariness are severe, so treating ethical egoism as identical to psychological egoism, as ordinary prudence, or as a defensible complete morality, misreads a challenging but widely rejected view.
origin: The normative ethical theory that one ought always to act in one's own self-interest, distinguished from descriptive psychological egoism and most associated in modern times with Ayn Rand's Objectivism.
